latest_nl_proof:
Let x be any real number, and write m = ⌊x⌋ and t = x - ⌊x⌋. Then t = frac(x), so x = m + t with m an integer and 0 ≤ t < 1.

Since m is an integer and k is a positive integer, km is also an integer. Therefore, for each k = 1, 2, ..., n,
⌊kx⌋ = ⌊k(m+t)⌋ = ⌊km + kt⌋ = km + ⌊kt⌋,
and similarly
⌊nx⌋ = nm + ⌊nt⌋.

Substituting these into the definition of f_n gives
f_n(x) = ⌊nx⌋ - \sum_{k=1}^n \frac{⌊kx⌋}{k}
= (nm + ⌊nt⌋) - \sum_{k=1}^n \frac{km + ⌊kt⌋}{k}.
Now simplify term by term:
\frac{km + ⌊kt⌋}{k} = m + \frac{⌊kt⌋}{k},
so
f_n(x) = nm + ⌊nt⌋ - \sum_{k=1}^n m - \sum_{k=1}^n \frac{⌊kt⌋}{k}
= nm + ⌊nt⌋ - nm - \sum_{k=1}^n \frac{⌊kt⌋}{k}
= ⌊nt⌋ - \sum_{k=1}^n \frac{⌊kt⌋}{k}.
But the right-hand side is exactly f_n(t), and t = frac(x). Hence
f_n(x) = f_n(frac(x)).

Since x was arbitrary, this holds for every real x.
role_in_parent: Reduces the maximization problem to the fundamental domain [0,1).
statement_nl: Let n be an integer greater than 1, and let f_n be defined by f_n(x) = floor(n*x) - sum_{k=1}^n floor(k*x)/k. For every real x, f_n(x) = f_n(frac(x)), where frac(x) = x - floor(x).

domain_restrictions: n is an integer and n > 1
k ranges over integers with 1 <= k <= n (implicit from the sum)
frac(x) is defined as x minus floor(x), so frac(x) lies in the interval from 0 up to but not including 1
statement_semantic_sketch.normalized_claim: For every integer n greater than 1, define f_n on real numbers by f_n(x) equals floor of n times x minus the sum from k equals 1 to n of (floor of k times x divided by k). Then for every real x, f_n(x) equals f_n(frac(x)), where frac(x) equals x minus floor(x).
quantifier_order: for all integers n with n > 1

variables.name: n
variables.role: fixed parameter for the function f_n; assumed greater than 1

variables.name: k
variables.role: summation index inside the definition of f_n

variables.name: x
variables.role: input variable to the function f_n

variables.role: value defined from n and floor expressions

variables.name: frac(x)

witness_dependencies: no existential witnesses; f_n is uniquely determined by n
